clinical_knowledge.topic: Acute Ascending Cholangitis (Reynolds' Pentad) evaluation and management
core_concepts: Prompt recognition and structured assessment of Acute Ascending Cholangitis (Reynolds' Pentad) is essential for guiding targeted diagnostic workup and clinical decision-making.
A thorough clinical history, baseline risk assessment, and targeted objective testing must be synthesized rather than relying on any single symptom in isolation.

Standard management emphasizes urgent sepsis resuscitation with IV fluids and broad-spectrum antibiotics, followed by emergent biliary decompression (ERCP, or percutaneous/surgical drainage if ERCP is unavailable), adapted to individual patient risk factors and clinical severity.
Diagnostic workup and therapeutic decisions should adhere to established clinical guidelines while accounting for patient-specific comorbidities.
diagnostic_clues: Chief Complaint: high fever, right upper abdominal pain, yellowing of skin, confusion, and low blood pressure

Key HPI features: 66F presenting with gallstone obstruction causing Charcot's triad plus hypotension and altered mental status (Reynolds' pentad). Requires urgent fluid resuscitation, IV antibiotics, and ERCP.

Objective/Exam findings: Fever, hypotension, and altered mental status (Reynolds' pentad) with jaundice and RUQ tenderness. Labs show leukocytosis and elevated bilirubin/alkaline phosphatase. Ultrasound or MRCP demonstrates a dilated common bile duct with choledocholithiasis.
Relevant background/PMH: No significant chronic medical history
common_misconceptions: Assuming that an atypical or mild presentation rules out Acute Ascending Cholangitis (Reynolds' Pentad).
Relying solely on a single normal laboratory value or imaging result to prematurely exclude pathology.
Equating temporary symptomatic relief with full resolution of the underlying condition without completing standard evaluation.
Misattributing symptoms exclusively to Acute cholecystitis without completing a comprehensive diagnostic workup.
dangerous_errors: Failing to recognize red-flag features and delaying urgent escalation or emergency intervention.
Prematurely discharging or reassuring the patient before completing appropriate diagnostic assessment.
Initiating empirical treatment without considering major patient contraindications or drug interactions.
Ignoring critical warning signs such as: Confusion and low blood pressure alongside jaundice and fever — Reynolds' pentad, needs urgent decompression.
management_principles: Initiate aggressive IV fluid resuscitation and broad-spectrum IV antibiotics covering enteric Gram-negatives and anaerobes immediately (sepsis bundle)
Closely monitor hemodynamics and mental status; escalate to ICU-level care if shock or worsening altered mental status persists
Obtain emergent biliary decompression via ERCP with sphincterotomy and stone extraction within 24 hours (or percutaneous transhepatic drainage/surgical decompression if ERCP is unavailable or fails)
boundaries_and_exceptions: Specific drug dosages, monitoring protocols, and referral criteria must be tailored to organ function, comorbidities, and local hospital pathways.
Atypical presentations in elderly, pediatric, or immunocompromised patients may require lower thresholds for inpatient monitoring and specialist consultation.

reference_soap.subjective: Patient presenting with symptoms of Acute Ascending Cholangitis Reynolds Pentad: high fever, right upper abdominal pain, yellowing of skin, confusion, and low blood pressure. 66F presenting with gallstone obstruction causing Charcot's triad plus hypotension and altered mental status (Reynolds' pentad). Requires urgent fluid resuscitation, IV antibiotics, and ERCP.
reference_soap.objective: Fever, hypotension, and altered mental status (Reynolds' pentad) with jaundice and RUQ tenderness. Labs show leukocytosis and elevated bilirubin/alkaline phosphatase. Ultrasound or MRCP demonstrates a dilated common bile duct with choledocholithiasis.
reference_soap.assessment: Acute Ascending Cholangitis with Reynolds' pentad (fever, jaundice, RUQ pain, hypotension, altered mental status) - a biliary sepsis emergency.
reference_soap.plan: 1. Aggressive IV fluid resuscitation and broad-spectrum IV antibiotics (sepsis bundle). 2. Close hemodynamic and mental status monitoring; escalate to ICU-level care if needed. 3. Emergent ERCP with sphincterotomy and stone extraction within 24 hours (or percutaneous/surgical decompression if ERCP is unavailable or fails).

learning_objectives: Distinguish Charcot's triad from the more severe Reynolds' pentad in ascending cholangitis
Prioritize sepsis resuscitation (IV fluids, broad-spectrum antibiotics) before definitive biliary drainage
Recognize the need for emergent biliary decompression via ERCP as the definitive treatment
Identify hemodynamic and mental status red flags that mandate ICU-level escalation

teaching.one_liner: Bacterial infection of an obstructed bile duct causing Charcot's triad (fever, jaundice, RUQ pain), and when shock and confusion are added, the more dangerous Reynolds' pentad.
red_flags: Confusion and low blood pressure alongside jaundice and fever — Reynolds' pentad, needs urgent decompression

must_ask.say: Have you had fever, yellowing of your skin or eyes, and pain under your right ribs?
Have you felt confused or less alert than usual?
When did the pain and fever start, and has it been getting worse?
Have you ever been told you have gallstones?
Has your urine become dark or your stool pale?

history.answer: I have a high fever and severe pain in the right side of my stomach, and I feel dizzy and confused.
The fever started yesterday morning, about twenty-four hours ago, and has been getting steadily worse.
My temperature climbed to 39 degrees Celsius at home, stays high constantly, and I have had severe shaking chills.
I took acetaminophen last night, but it barely lowered the temperature and the stomach pain did not improve.
I have no cough, phlegm, or throat irritation, though I have been breathing a bit faster because of the fever.
I have no pain or burning when urinating, no urinary frequency, and no aching in my back or flanks.
The pain is a constant, severe ache in my upper right abdomen, and I threw up twice yesterday afternoon.
I do not have a stiff neck or a headache, but my head feels hazy, and I have trouble thinking clearly today.
My husband noticed earlier today that my eyes and skin have turned noticeably yellow.
My urine has turned very dark like strong tea, and my stool this morning looked pale and grayish.
I have not seen any rashes, black crusty scabs, or insect bites on my skin.
I have not had drenching night sweats before yesterday, and my weight has remained completely stable.
I have not felt any swollen glands or lumps in my neck, underarms, or groin.
I have not traveled overseas recently, done any hiking or farm work, or handled any animals.
Nobody in my household or workplace has had a fever or similar illness recently.
I have never received chemotherapy, steroids, or any medicines that weaken the immune system.
I do not have heart disease or artificial heart valves, and I have not had dental procedures recently.
I have not started any new prescription drugs recently.
I have had only my husband as a partner and have never used intravenous or illicit drugs.
Several years ago, an ultrasound for a health checkup showed small gallstones, but they never caused symptoms.
I thought I just caught a terrible stomach flu or food poisoning, but now everything feels foggy and yellow.
I'm so scared my liver is failing completely, because my older sister died in a coma after turning yellow.
I have no chronic medical conditions such as high blood pressure, diabetes, or liver disease.
I have never undergone any surgical operations or hospitalizations.
I do not take any daily prescription medications, over-the-counter medicines, or health supplements.
I do not have any known allergies to medications, foods, or materials.
I have never smoked cigarettes in my life.
I drink only an occasional glass of wine, once or twice a month at most.
I work full-time in an office as an accountant and live with my husband in an apartment.
No one in my immediate family has had chronic liver disease, gallstones, or gastrointestinal cancers.
I went through natural menopause over fifteen years ago and have had no vaginal bleeding since.

exam.finding: Ill-appearing, lethargic woman with flushed skin, diaphoresis, and noticeable cutaneous jaundice.
Blood pressure 85/55 mmHg, pulse 118 beats/min, respiratory rate 22 breaths/min, body temperature 39.2 C, oxygen saturation 96% on room air.
Patient is somnolent and oriented only to person, responding slowly with confused answers.
Obvious scleral icterus bilaterally; conjunctivae are not pale.
Dry mucous membranes with icteric sublingual tissue; pharynx is not injected and tonsils are normal.
Clear breath sounds bilaterally without wheezes, rales, or rhonchi.
Tachycardic regular rhythm without murmurs, rubs, or gallops.
Marked tenderness on palpation in the right upper quadrant and epigastrium without involuntary guarding.
Inspiratory arrest upon deep palpation of the right upper quadrant (positive Murphy sign).
Generalized jaundice and warm, flushed skin without petechiae, purpura, rash, or eschar.
Supple neck without nuchal rigidity, Kernig sign, or Brudzinski sign.
